Three major US banks just changed their terms: if an AI agent gets hacked, the loss is yours.

Citi, PNC and Citizens updated their terms this week. Customers are now responsible for anything a third-party AI agent does in their accounts, even after leaked credentials or a hacked agent. JPMorgan and Bank of America reportedly went first.

Read that again as a developer.

Agents are getting real access to money, data and infrastructure. Nobody has agreed yet on who's liable when one goes wrong.

What I'd build into any agent feature today:

• Least-privilege access, read-only by default
• Hard limits on spending and actions
• Human approval for anything irreversible
• A full audit log of every action
• Short-lived tokens, never long-lived passwords

The next big skill isn't building agents that can do more. It's building agents that can safely do less.

When an AI agent makes a costly mistake, who should pay: the user, the company, or the developer who built it? 👇

#AIAgents #AISecurity #SoftwareEngineering #Cybersecurity #ArtificialIntelligence

Credit score choice is here for conventional loans, but adoption in pricing is still thin.
What's confirmed:• Since Sept. 9, all Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac approved lenders may use VantageScore 4.0 or Classic FICO on eligible loans, one model per loan (FHFA).• Both models have used one LLPA grid since Oct. 1; the earlier 20-point VantageScore adjustment is gone.• Bank of America Global Research (reported by HousingWire, Nov. 16): 173 sellers delivered loans with a VantageScore 4.0 score pulled in early November, but only ~8% of October conventional issuance was priced with it; Rocket and UWM account for ~95% of those.• FHA accepts FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 alongside Classic FICO for case numbers assigned on or after Jan. 1, 2027 (ML 2026-11). Fannie Mae said Nov. 18 it's preparing for FICO 10T, which is not yet deliverable.
For Realtors and clients: ask which score model will price the loan, whether the loan type allows it, and have the quote reflect that model. A new model doesn't guarantee a higher score or lower rate.

Los bancos de EE. UU. se cayeron y todos pensaron en un ciberataque. ¿Su empresa sabría la diferencia?

Esta semana, clientes de Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank y Zelle experimentaron fallas en aplicaciones y servicios digitales que rápidamente generaron preocupación y especulaciones sobre un posible ciberataque masivo.

Sin embargo, la causa fue otra: un error de software.

Días después, la historia dio un giro inesperado. JPMorgan Chase confirmó un incidente de seguridad real, pero no en sus sistemas bancarios centrales. El ataque afectó a proveedores externos que administraban información de marketing y pudo haber expuesto nombres y correos electrónicos de algunos clientes. 

💡 Este caso deja una reflexión importante para cualquier organización:

Desde la perspectiva de un cliente, una falla tecnológica y un ciberataque pueden verse exactamente igual. En ambos casos hay incertidumbre, interrupciones del servicio, preocupación por la información y posibles impactos reputacionales.

La diferencia está en cómo responde la organización.

Las empresas deben estar preparadas para identificar rápidamente si enfrentan un problema operativo o un incidente de ciberseguridad, activar los procedimientos adecuados.

Además, este caso vuelve a poner sobre la mesa un riesgo cada vez más relevante: la seguridad de los terceros. Aunque la infraestructura principal de una organización no sea comprometida, un proveedor con acceso a información sensible puede convertirse en el origen de un incidente con impacto reputacional y regulatorio. 

💙 En CAVALTEC ayudamos a las organizaciones a fortalecer su capacidad de prevención, detección y respuesta mediante:

🔹 Evaluaciones de proveedores críticos, identificando riesgos y oportunidades de mejora en terceros con acceso a información o sistemas sensibles.
🔹 Autoevaluación de Ciberseguridad, para medir el nivel de madurez de la organización e identificar brechas frente a buenas prácticas y estándares reconocidos.
🔹 Ciberseguridad 360, que permite gestionar activos, riesgos, controles y hallazgos desde una visión centralizada.

Microsoft. FAA. Banks. NSA. America’s systems are going down one by one. Who’s pulling the plug?

🎙️ Who Unplugged America? Out now.

Kingdom of Fear and Frozen Terminals: Dispatches from the Great Banking Chokepoint of November ’26

You don’t need a badge or a warrant anymore to lock down an entire country—just a quiet glitch in the clearinghouse and a population dumb enough to leave its cash at home.
Around 11:30 a.m. Eastern on Monday, November 16, the digital leash snapped tight. Anyone at a checkout counter trying to tap a card or push a Zelle transfer got a sudden lesson in who holds the keys to their money. JPMorgan Chase choked on its own wires, sending nearly 5,000 enraged customers banging on the digital glass as balances vanished, teller windows went dead, and payments froze in limbo. Because this bloated, hyper-consolidated casino is wired together with baling wire, the contagion immediately burned customers at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One, Truist, and Zelle whenever their money crossed Chase's paralyzed rails.
Watch the official playbook unfold:
 * The Alibi: By 4:00 p.m., Chase blamed a "temporary software bug in an on-premise hardware system"—swearing it wasn't a cyberattack while millions couldn't move a dime until Monday night.
 * The Cascade: This choke-out hit dead-center in a seven-day meltdown that buckled Microsoft 365, grounded the FAA nationwide, and knocked Apple and the NSA's internal networks offline the very next day.
 * The Kicker: Just 72 hours after denying hackers were involved, Chase, Visa, and Mastercard admitted today that third-party vendors were hit by a cyberattack—right as the extortion gang n0n put all three on a 48-hour leak countdown. Naturally, they claim it only touched "marketing data."
They call it seamless fintech; in reality, it is a single-point-of-failure chokehold where the house controls the switch.
Keep some folding green in your pocket. Don't trust the cloud to feed you. And never buy the first press release.

Gave an AI your bank login? Your bank says anything it does is on you.

Citi updated its Online User Agreement in November 2026 to add Section H, on third-party AI agents. The agreement covers consumers, sole proprietors and eligible small businesses. What it says:

• Citi cautions customers against using any third-party AI agent to access their accounts — including handing the agent information, instructions or transactions.
• If you give an agent your Online Credentials anyway, Citi will consider any access and actions taken by the agent as authorised by you.
• That includes credentials that are further shared or leaked: anything done with them still counts as authorised by you.
• Citi takes no duty to investigate, even if the agent's actions conflict with the prompts or instructions you gave it. Agent errors, misinterpretation and exceeding authority are the customer's responsibility, and monitoring the agent is the customer's job — not the bank's.
• Permitting access also authorises disclosure of your information, including sensitive personal information, to the agent — and Citi's Privacy Notice does not apply to the agent. Citi may also cut off agent access at any time, without notice. The section does not apply to AI tools Citi itself provides.

Citi is the case read first-hand. As reported by TechCrunch (Nov 18): PNC changed its terms the same week, Citizens emailed customers a similar warning, and JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies last month. No loss or breach case is reported, and whether these clauses survive a consumer-protection dispute is untested.

The game plan:
1. Never give a third-party AI agent your bank login. If a tool can't connect through a bank-approved, read-only or token-based route, that is the answer.
2. Prefer your bank's own AI tools, read-only connections, and tokenised payments with a hard cap and a confirm-before-buy step.
3. Read your own bank's AI-agent terms and ask, in writing, how beyond-instructions or leaked-credential transactions are treated. Don't assume Canadian banks match Citi — either way.
4. Already shared credentials? Change the password from a clean device, revoke access, turn on transaction alerts, and review activity line by line.
5. Brief anyone with access to your business accounts — a shared business login carries the same treatment.

Full story + sources: https://lnkd.in/gWEr66qp
